title: Alarms, Fault Context and Maintenance Escalation

content.overview: A technician does not need to diagnose every failure, but must capture useful fault context, complete permitted checks and escalate conditions without repeatedly resetting or masking alarms.

vocabulary.definition: A system indication that a measured or controlled condition met a defined alert or fault condition.
An observed effect of a problem that does not by itself establish the root cause.
Information about what, where, when and under what conditions an equipment problem occurred.

sections.title: An alarm is evidence, not a diagnosis
sections.body: Record the alarm, asset, zone, time, readings, visible symptoms and relevant work context. Similar symptoms can have different causes, so technicians should not declare a root cause without supporting evidence.

sections.title: Create a maintenance-ready escalation
sections.body: Perform only the operator checks allowed by the SOP. A useful escalation describes the asset, location, time, observed condition, alarm or reading, safe action taken and affected production area. If the next step requires servicing or hazardous access, stop and refer it.

workedExamples: A pump alarm and dry zone are documented with asset and location before escalation rather than repeatedly reset.
An abnormal fan sound is reported with time, asset and observed condition before the fan fails completely.
commonMistakes: Resetting an alarm repeatedly to make it disappear.
Writing only 'broken' without asset, time, location or observed condition.
content.practicalApplication: Create a maintenance escalation record from a simulated alarm packet containing equipment identity, controller status, room assignment and worker observations.
content.summary: Good fault reporting converts observations into actionable information. Technicians capture context, complete only permitted checks and escalate unresolved equipment conditions.

blocks.title: An alarm tells you a condition occurred; it does not prove why
blocks.body: A displayed alarm, abnormal sound, missing flow, high reading, or other symptom is useful evidence. Similar symptoms can come from different causes. Technician I should capture reproducible context and perform only the checks allowed by the operator procedure rather than converting an early observation into an unsupported root-cause statement.

blocks.alt: Annotated maintenance-ready fault report showing asset and location, time, alarm or observation, permitted checks and results, process or crop impact, safe action and notification, with a warning against vague statements such as 'pump broken' and unsupported root-cause claims.
blocks.caption: A useful maintenance escalation gives the next qualified person enough context to reproduce and investigate the condition.

blocks.title: Observation, permitted check, and hypothesis are different
rows: Record directly with asset, location, time, and relevant reading or condition
Reservoir level verified normal under the operator SOP
Record the check and result; do not imply a deeper diagnosis
Scheduled Zone 3 irrigation did not occur
State the affected process or crop area
Possible internal pump or valve problem
Only include if useful/allowed and label it unconfirmed
Confirmed failed component or control logic

blocks.title: The reset clears the alarm for five minutes
blocks.setting: A pump alarm appears. A permitted operator reset clears it, but the alarm returns twice and one irrigation zone remains dry. The SOP does not authorize opening the pump or panel.
options: Keep resetting until the irrigation event finishes
Open the pump because the recurring alarm proves an internal blockage
Capture the recurring alarm and zone impact, complete only permitted checks, leave the asset/status controlled under procedure, and escalate with the fault context
Delete the alarm history after the reset succeeds
blocks.answer: Capture the recurring alarm and zone impact, complete only permitted checks, leave the asset/status controlled under procedure, and escalate with the fault context.
blocks.feedback: Repeatedly masking the alarm can hide a persistent condition. The technician should preserve the evidence and stop at the operator boundary.

blocks.title: Maintenance-ready escalation record
blocks.description: Capture facts that help the qualified receiving role investigate without needing the technician to diagnose the system.

fields.label: Asset / location
fields.value: Exact equipment identifier, zone, room, or work area

fields.label: Time
fields.value: When the alarm or symptom occurred and whether it repeated

fields.label: Alarm / symptom
fields.value: Exact displayed alarm, sound, reading, no-flow condition, leak, or other observed effect

fields.label: Relevant readings
fields.value: Permitted values or indicators available at the time

fields.label: Permitted checks
fields.value: Operator-level checks performed and their results

fields.label: Process / crop impact
fields.value: What work, zone, material, or schedule was affected

fields.label: Safe action
fields.value: Out-of-service status, pause, isolation where authorized, or other controlled response

fields.label: Notification / ticket
fields.value: Who was notified and the maintenance/deviation record if applicable

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Optional unconfirmed idea, clearly separated from observed fact

blocks.title: Turn an alarm packet into a useful escalation
blocks.instructions: Use a simulated controller screenshot, equipment ID, room map, time sequence, and operator observations to create a maintenance-ready report.
prompts: Extract only facts directly supported by the packet.
List operator checks that are explicitly permitted.
Identify the production or crop impact.
Separate any reasonable hypothesis from the confirmed observations.
State the point where additional work crosses into servicing or hazardous access.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Good technicians do not need to guess every root cause. They make the fault legible: what happened, where, when, what was checked, what was affected, what safe action was taken, and what remains for the authorized investigator.
